# #lock Protocol

**How to use this file:** Step-by-step checklist for when Justin says `#lock` or it's time for a checkpoint. Follow the steps in order.

**Do not edit this file without Justin's approval.** Propose changes; don't make them directly.

---

**Before writing anything below, re-read and follow `docs/protocols/ac-writing-protocol.md`.** A #lock produces multiple writes to persistent files in rapid succession — current-state, CHANGELOG, ARCHITECTURE, the BUILD doc, session docs. If you don't have the writing protocol fresh, you'll make exactly the mistakes it exists to prevent — stale edits on shared files, missing truncation canaries, over-compressed context — that corrupt files other instances depend on.

When Justin says `#lock` or it's time for a checkpoint:

1. **`CHANGELOG.md` (per-repo)** — Add brief one-liners for anything built or changed this session, **to the `CHANGELOG.md` of each repo the change touched.** Changelogs are per-repo: the responsible AC owns the entry and routes it to every repo the change actually hit (the **cross-repo rule**); a change that touched `_evryn-meta` also goes in the meta changelog (every AC reads that on load). Log *substantive ships/changes*, never session narration — the full "what belongs / who writes / routing" rule is in each `CHANGELOG.md` header. *(First on purpose: with the changelogs fresh in hand, the current-state refresh below can safely move shipped items *out* — the changelog is the record that makes a cut safe.)*
2. **Deploy log (`docs/deploy-log.md`) — if a production deploy (`railway up`) happened this session, record it.** The deploy ledger is the single source of truth for *what shipped to prod, when, under which version.* Add a new **`v0.2.N`** row (newest-first) with the date, the deployed commit + its **git tag**, and a one-line "what shipped"; and confirm the matching `git tag v0.2.N` is on the deployed commit in `evryn-backend` (push it). The **ledger + an item's STATUS are the authoritative pair** for "did X ship?" — a *"riding round/wave-X"* tag is intent, never proof (this is the exact gap that made the determination-sharing guardrail look shipped when it wasn't). Also bump `docs/current-state.md`'s "Live deploy" line to the new version. **No prod deploy this session → skip this step.** (The version convention — one `v0.2.N` bump per prod `railway up`, no leading zero, git-tagged — lives in `docs/deploy-log.md`'s header.)
3. **`docs/current-state.md`** — Refresh to reflect current reality. **Clean snapshot, not a log:** fold your update *into* the snapshot — don't append a new dated `*Updated:*` stamp on top of the old ones. When something has shipped or been superseded, it moves *out* of here and into `CHANGELOG.md` / `deploy-log.md`.

   **Keep it current — but flag-don't-delete what you can't confirm.** If something looks clearly stale *and* the changelog / deploy-log / runtime confirms it shipped or died, cut it — that's good hygiene, and those records are what make it safe to cut. But if you **don't know** whether an item is still live (it may be another instance's in-flight lane you lack context on), **flag it to Justin — don't delete it.** Removing a peer's still-live state because you didn't recognize it is worse than leaving one stale line.

   **Reconcile the OTHER direction too — did a ship get MISSED?** Beyond cutting stale items, scan the **recent entries in the relevant repos' changelogs** (+ the meta changelog) *and* the **runtime** (git log / deployed state) for anything that shipped but current-state doesn't reflect. **A ship can creep down the changelog unseen while current-state lags** — that's the failure that leaves agents not realizing something's already done (and re-proposing it a month later). If current-state is missing a recent ship, add it. *(current-state is the load-in snapshot; the changelog + runtime are ground truth — keep the snapshot honest against both.)*
4. **Founding Team current-state** — AC is the ambassador for the build (DC/QC/OC don't write here; AC represents self + them). **Append** to the *end* of `evryn-team-workspace/shared/current-state/current-state.md` — never overwrite. Start your entry with your name (AC, AC0, AC1) and a proper timestamp: `**<your instance> — <full ISO timestamp>:**` — e.g. `**AC1 — 2026-06-13T16:52:57-07:00:**` (or just `**AC — …:**` if you're unnumbered). **Avoid self-descriptor additions unless absolutely necessary** — e.g. `AC2 (BUILD doc realignment)`. The team will sometimes need to do this, because there might be two Sorens working at once — but this extra labeling is rarely necessary for an AC, because that's what the numbering convention is for.

    **Keep it SHORT — a few lines.** The appendage has had a tendency to balloon into a build log; it is not one. The audience is the **whole founding team** (Lucas, Emma, Mira, Marlowe, Nathan, Thea, Soren) + Justin, reading at *their* altitude — most never touch the code.

    **The test for every line:** *"Would the non-technical members of the team think or act differently because of this?"* If a line only means something to someone reading the runtime, it belongs in `_evryn-meta/docs/current-state.md` (Soren reads that for build depth) — **not here.**

    > ### 🔴 AND THE SAME TEST IN REVERSE — this is the direction that actually bites, and it has now bitten twice
    >
    > *(Sharpened 2026-09-02 on Justin's ruling. The rule above already existed and runs only one way; the failure runs the other way.)*
    >
    > 🔑 **`_evryn-meta/docs/current-state.md` is read by BUILD agents. The founding team does not read it, and does not write to it.** ⇒ **If something is FOR a founding-team member — a question for Soren, something Mira needs to decide, anything addressed to a person rather than to a lane — it goes in the TEAM current-state — or sometimes as a note in one team-member's memory (but this **always** has to go through Justin) — but either way it never goes in the meta one.**
    >
    > ⚠️ **Why this is worse than it sounds, and why it earns a rule rather than a preference: it fails as a SILENT non-delivery.** **The writer sees a durable, committed, correctly-formatted entry and reasonably concludes the message was delivered. The intended reader never opens that file.** ⇒ **Nobody discovers it, because from the sending side it looks exactly like success.** 🔑 **Same family as the mailbox rule that *committing is sending* — writing something down is not the same as putting it where its reader will be.**
    >
    > ⭐ **The one-question version, and it is the reverse of the test above:** ***is this addressed to an operations (founding) team member, or to an AC/whoever is next in the build?*** **A team member → the team file. AC/build → the meta file.**
    - **IN:** what shipped at the *product* level, what's blocked and why the team should care, big movements (go-live progress, a major decision, a constraint everyone holds).
    - **OUT:** file/function names, commit SHAs, deploy IDs, QC finding labels, the build play-by-play. **Naming a runtime file/function or a SHA *as build detail* is the smell — if you're doing that, you're very likely writing the wrong doc.** (The nuance: a *pointer/link to a doc the reader should go open* — e.g. linking the active sprint doc so the team can find it — is the exception, and is often right. The bar is *play-by-play build detail* vs. *a signpost to where the fuller picture lives*.)

    Target: one short paragraph or 2-4 tight bullets.
5. **Doc-currency gate — the docs that describe the running system (hard gate: #lock isn't complete until this is *answered*).** For EACH doc below, answer explicitly: *did this session change what it claims about the system?* For every "yes," either **update it now** or **route it** (name the section + owner). A deliberate *"no change"* is a valid logged answer, but a silent skip is not. Use `docs/protocols/doc-update-routing-protocol.md` for the exact "which change → which section, and what AC edits directly vs. routes to an owner" mapping — so this is a *lookup*, not a memory exercise (it also names the *other* surfaces a change can reach, several of which are their own steps below). **⚠ The architecture/build/sprint docs have been going stale — give this real attention, not a skim.**
    - a. **The active sprint doc** — mark completed steps DONE, add new steps, reshape. (DC/QC don't write here.)
    - b. **The active build doc** — flip phase badges to match what actually shipped; if it carries an "Active session" pointer and that session content is now absorbed into persistent docs, clear the pointer. 
    - c. **The relevant architecture doc** — status badges + prose still match the runtime. Remember **built ≠ merged ≠ deployed** — don't flip a badge to "live" on a mere merge; a config-gated ship reads *"shipped, inert until `<FLAG>`,"* not "live."
    - d. **🔴 The Code Atlas — did this session change the runtime's SHAPE?** A module moved, split, renamed, added or deleted; a dependency edge created or removed. If yes, **the Atlas must already reflect it** — the standing order (CLAUDE.md, Documentation Approach) is that an Atlas update rides the *build*, not the checkpoint, because only the person who moved the code knows what moved. **So this step is an AUDIT, not the place to do the work:** if a shape change shipped this session without its Atlas update, that is a gap to close now *and* a process miss to name, not a routine catch-up. **Why it is a hard gate rather than hygiene:** the Atlas exists to be trusted, so a stale one does not fail loudly — an agent reasons confidently from a map of a system that no longer exists, which is worse than having no map at all. 📍 *(The Atlas is `evryn-backend/docs/atlas/` — 12 sections, a complete non-overlapping partition of every `src/` file plus the identity half, merged to `main`. Start at `00-INDEX.md`, which states each section's exact file set.)*
    - e. **Learnings to their RIGHT HOME (the persist-learnings standing order — CLAUDE.md). 🔴 THE LOCAL HALF GOES FIRST, AND IT GOES NOW.** Did this session *teach* something durable — how to reason about a codebase, a recurring failure mode, a design constraint you only learned by hitting it? Route it by altitude: **architectural** (a property of the system, e.g. "this runtime punishes local reasoning") → the ARCHITECTURE doc; **build-mechanics** → the BUILD doc; **this-sprint** → the sprint/tracker; **only the GENERALIZABLE version — the one another repo, holding a different codebase, could act on** → `LEARNINGS.md` (**step 11 carries the mechanics; this bullet owns the routing decision** — ⚠️ `AGENT_PATTERNS.md` was collapsed into `LEARNINGS.md` 2026-08-12 and retired 2026-08-19; it no longer exists, so never route there). A handoff is where a learning is first captured, **never** where it lives — if the only place it exists is a session/handoff doc, it hasn't been persisted.
      - 🔴 **WHY LOCAL-FIRST IS A HARD ORDERING AND NOT A PREFERENCE (Justin, 2026-08-13).** `LEARNINGS.md` is **drained at `#sweep`, and `#sweep` can be weeks away** — as of this writing it had not run in 20 days against a weekly cadence. **So filing a lane-local lesson there does not merely mis-shelve it: it puts a thing YOUR OWN BUILD NEEDS NOW behind a queue nobody will read until long after you needed it — while everyone believes it was captured.** That is the recorded-but-never-delivered failure arriving through the door marked *"I wrote it down."* **The lesson for today's build folds in TODAY. Figuring out where else it might inform is what `#sweep` is for.**
      - **The test, cheap enough to run per learning:** strip every name, path, SHA and date from your session. **Is there a rule left that a reader in another repo could act on?** If yes, *that rule* is the `LEARNINGS.md` entry — state it first, then the minimum evidence, then a pointer to where the full forensics live. **If no, it is not a cross-project learning at all. Route it local and stop.** ⚠️ **Both halves are often true of one lesson** — the local version local, the general version there. **And polishing a purely-local lesson into general language makes it WORSE**, because it launders something local into a false generality another repo might act on.
      - ⚠️ **Do NOT over-correct into abstraction.** The agent that read all 89 collapsed `AGENT_PATTERNS` entries found that the only ones it could prove *false* were the ones carrying dates and specifics: ***"a file optimized purely for transferability becomes a file of unfalsifiable claims that quietly rot."*** **Keep enough provenance to make an entry checkable later.**

    **Why this gate exists:** drift accumulated here for months (a shipped feature whose "blocker" badge never flipped — nearly triggering duplicate build work; a renamed table the docs never caught up to) until a full-history reconciliation was needed; this gate is the prevention.
6. **Identity files (`evryn-backend/identity/`) — their own review protocol.** If this session produced or merged any change under that path — Evryn's `core.md`, `situations/*`, `activities/*`, `internal-reference/*`, `public-knowledge/*` — the change goes through `evryn-team-workspace/shared/protocols/identity-file-review.md` (branch + PR + reviewer + checklist + `#dev-alerts` ping on merge). AC is the default reviewer. Confirm here that the protocol was followed; Mira is the owner of identity docs, so if you authored or merged identity-file content yourself, make sure either Mira and/or Justin signed off on it.
7. **Hub & spokes** — If anything this session changes company-level truth (Hub) or domain depth (spokes), update them (the Hub is Justin's — make sure he is able to vet in SCM before any commit). Also check: if a spoke was modified, does the Hub's corresponding section still set the right expectation?

   **Company-context module.** If the Hub changed substantively, its **public-safe derivative — the `evryn_knowledge` `company-context` DB row — must be refreshed** (route to Justin/Lucas). Easy to miss because it's a DB row, not a file.
8. **Cross-runtime safety propagation.** *Did this session close a **security or safety-boundary** hole in ANY runtime we operate?* (Not an ordinary bug — an auth gate, an isolation boundary, an approval gate, a dormancy/kill switch, an egress guard.) We build these runtimes in parallel *in different lanes*, and each lane reviews only its own diff — **so a hole closed in one silently re-grows in another unless someone with the cross-lane view checks.** A deliberate *"no security/safety hole closed this session"* is a valid logged answer; **a silent skip is not.**

   **If yes — do this, in this order:**

   1. 🔴 **NAME THE CLASS, not the bug.** The class is what travels; the instance does not. *(Worked example, 2026-08-12: not "`notify.ts` leaked a webhook URL" but **"a caught error stringified into a log or outbound message, where the error object embeds a credential-bearing URL"** — which is checkable in a codebase you have never read.)*
   2. 🔴 **ASK THE CONDUCTOR WHO OWNS THAT RUNTIME. Do NOT go searching it yourself.** *(Justin's ruling, 2026-08-12: the old wording said "check that class against every other runtime," which reads as an instruction to go read a codebase you do not hold — **"otherwise someone might burn a bunch of tokens searching, and I don't want that."**)* **Send a peer message naming the class, your evidence, and what a "no" would have to rule out.** They are live in that runtime with the context you lack; an answer that costs them two minutes costs you an afternoon.
      - **The mechanism, since there is no live AC-to-AC delivery:** a **committed file** both parties can see (`_evryn-meta/CLAUDE.md`, Multi-instance awareness) — or route through Justin, who will hand it to the right instance. **Proven 2026-08-12: a coordination file plus a polling monitor produced a verified cross-runtime answer in minutes.**
      - ⚠️ **Say explicitly that you are asking, not delegating** — *"if this is more than a few minutes, say so and I will spin an agent instead."* A peer conductor is not your report and does not owe you work.
   3. **Only if there is NO conductor for that runtime, or they cannot take it, spin an AC subagent** with the class and the evidence. **That is the expensive path, not the default.**
   4. **A pending answer does NOT block the `#lock`, but it must be RECORDED as pending** — in your handoff, naming who you asked and what you asked. **An unanswered propagation check that nobody is holding is the same as a skipped one.**

   **And be honest with yourself about why step 2 exists:** if this session closed a significant safety boundary, **you are deep in *your* runtime's context and you almost certainly lack the information to judge its relevance elsewhere.** Confidence here is not evidence. **The person who already holds that codebase is a better instrument than any amount of your own searching.**
9. **Decisions** — If decisions were made this session, determine if they're session level or architectural. If only session level, ensure they're captured in the session or working doc. Session docs are disposable — absorb and archive/delete, so if they are more permanent, ensure they're captured into persistent docs. **If any decisions this session are architectural (change how the system works, not just craft/process choices), write them as ADRs now — decisions captured only in session docs often get lost in the shuffle over time**.
9b. **🔴 RULINGS — every decision Justin made this session gets a DURABLE HOME OUTSIDE YOUR HANDOFF, and its wording agreed with him before it lands.** *(Justin's ruling, 2026-08-21.)*
    > **The gap this closes:** the routing protocol has a home for a *learning*, a *decision about the system*, *state*, and *build detail*. **It had no row for *"Justin ruled something about how we work"*** — so a ruling landed in whatever handoff was open, got copied into the next one, and was eventually reconstructed forensically by someone who was not there, **if it was found at all.**
    - **For each ruling you recorded this session, answer explicitly: does this exist anywhere OUTSIDE this handoff?** ⚠️ **"Carried into the next handoff" is NOT a durable home — it is the same countdown, restarted.**
    - **Where it goes: `docs/protocols/doc-update-routing-protocol.md`, change-type 9.** **Do not keep a second list here; that is the drift this step exists to kill.**
    - 🔴 **AGREE THE WORDING WITH HIM BEFORE IT IS PERSISTED.** **Many rulings are situation-specific, and a generalized version may need real modification — or may be wrong.** **Bring him the exact text and the destination, in a form he can answer with *agree* or *adjust*.**
      > 📌 **The worked example, and it is why this rule exists:** *"He does NOT review merges"* was recorded as standing. **What he meant was *"I can't review CODE — I'm not an engineer."*** **Read out of its moment, it says he reviews nothing — which is false, and would have removed his vet from every prose file in the estate.**
10. **Retire stale session & working docs — but surface before moving. Every session doc you worked with must either get RETIRED, or carry its hold condition IN ITS OWN FIRST FEW LINES.** *(Justin's design, 2026-08-21.)*

    > ### 🔴 THREE DISPOSITIONS, NOT TWO — and SUPERSEDE is the DEFAULT for a doc that has been corrected
    >
    > *(Justin's ruling, 2026-09-01.)* ⚠️ **This step was written as a binary: retire, or hold with a banner. A doc whose lane is genuinely still live has only ONE of those available to it** — so it gets held, and then it accretes corrections, and **nothing in this checklist ever catches that.** **The banner's aging check asks whether the CONDITION is still satisfiable. It never asks whether the DOCUMENT is still accurate about itself.**
    >
    > **1 · RETIRE** — the work is finished. Archive it. ⭐ **A retired doc's staleness is HARMLESS**: nobody reads `historical/` expecting current truth, and the frozen-record rule already forbids correcting it. **Staleness stops being a problem the moment retirement is confirmed.**
    > **2 · SUPERSEDE** — the work continues, but the doc has **LAYERED**. **Archive this one and write a fresh one stating current truth in a SINGLE layer.** 🔴 **This is the default whenever the trigger below fires.**
    > **3 · CARRY** — the doc is still accurate and un-layered. Keep it — **and bring it FULLY CURRENT in this same set-down.** ⚠️ **A carried doc that is not current is a DEFECT, not a state.**
    >
    > ### 🔴 HOW TO ARCHIVE — two rules, and the whole findability promise rests on them
    >
    > *(Justin's ruling, 2026-09-02, after an audit found twelve archived docs that the findability rule could not reach.)*
    >
    > **① Unless there's a compelling reason, vetted explicitly by Justin, NEVER CHANGE THE FILENAME. Not the date, not one character.** **The ONLY thing that changes when a doc is retired is its LOCATION.** 🔑 **This is not tidiness — it is the entire mechanism.** **Whatever a doc was called while it was in play is exactly what it is called in the archive**, so a stale reference anywhere in the estate still names the file correctly. ⚠️ **If you want to record *when it was archived*, put a BANNER INSIDE the file. Never encode it in the name.**
    >
    > **② FILE IT UNDER THE DOC'S OWN DATE — the one at the front of its filename — NEVER today's.** `docs/sessions/historical/YYYY.MM/`, where `YYYY.MM` comes from **the document**, not from the calendar on the day you are archiving it.
    >
    > ⚠️ **RULE ② IS THE ONE THAT IS EASY TO INADVERTENTLY BREAK, and it breaks because the wrong answer feels natural.** *"Archive this"* can read as *"put it in the current bin,"* so an agent retiring a June doc in July can be tempted to file it under July.
    >
    > ### 🔎 AND THEREFORE — HOW TO FIND A RETIRED DOC: SEARCH BY NAME, NOT BY PATH
    >
    > **Because the name never changes, you never have to reconstruct a path or know which folder someone chose:**
    > ```bash
    > git ls-files "*<filename-fragment>*"
    > ```
    > ⭐ **This is strictly more robust than reasoning from the date, and that is why it is the rule rather than a convenience:** it survives a misfiled folder, it survives any future change to how we organize `historical/`, and **it is the only thing that works for the handful of archived files that carry no date prefix at all.** ⚠️ **A date-based lookup fails on all three of those and fails SILENTLY — the searcher concludes the document is gone.**
    >
    > ### 🔑 THE TRIGGER — it is self-announcing, which is the only reason it will actually fire
    >
    > > **The moment you write a correction that points at ANOTHER SECTION OF THE SAME DOCUMENT, that document needs SUPERSEDING — not another correction.**
    >
    > ⭐ **What it deliberately does NOT trigger on: ADDITION.** **Appending a new finding is growth and is fine.** **Correcting an earlier statement is layering.** ⇒ **One testable question: does this new text tell the reader to DISTRUST older text in the same file?** **Yes → supersede. No → carry on.**
    >
    > ⚠️ **Why layering is worse than it looks, and why "just fix it in place" does not work.** A corrected doc acquires a **READ ORDER** — a preamble telling you which of its own sections to believe — and a fresh instance then spends its first hour deciding which layer wins, **which is the exact cost the doc existed to remove.** 🔴 **And a correction filed in ONE place does not neutralise a stale instruction elsewhere in the same file:** one lane added a corrections table and considered the job done; a second pass found the file still handing a reader a wrong cadence and a dead address, **in numbered, paste-ready steps.**
    >
    > ### ⭐ WHY SUPERSEDE IS SAFE HERE WHEN REWRITING IS NORMALLY BARRED — two rules already in force make it nearly free, and neither was adopted for this
    >
    > 1. **The superseded doc is ARCHIVED, never deleted.** ⇒ **A rewrite that drops something is RECOVERABLE — the original is still in `historical/`.** 🔑 **That is precisely what makes rewriting SAFER than compressing in place**, which `ac-writing-protocol.md` warns against for exactly the drop-something reason. **The archive is the safety net that the in-place edit does not have.** Having said that, it is *critical* that you make sure the superseding doc captures what it needs. **Skimping on this is a *very common* failure mode, and even though the correct info is available in the superseded doc, that's *invisible* when reading the superseding doc**.
    > 2. 🔑 **Session-doc references are no longer repointed when a doc moves.** ⇒ **Superseding breaks no inbound pointer, because inbound pointers were already expected to go stale.** **Without that rule this would be expensive; with it, the cost is one file.**
    >
    > ⚠️ **THE ONE REPOINT THAT MUST HAPPEN — and it is NOT a falsification of a frozen record:** add **`SUPERSEDED BY: <path>`** to the top of the archived doc. **It is an archival annotation, not a correction to a claim**, so the frozen-record rule does not bar it — and it is the only thing that lets a reader who followed a stale pointer reach the live doc.
    > ### 🔒 THE HOLD BANNER — one line, at the top of the held doc itself
    > ```
    > 🔒 **HELD-SESSION-DOC** — <why it is alive, one line> · **RETIRE UPON:** <testable condition> · **OWNER:** <LINEAGE, e.g. ACP / ACT> · **HELD SINCE:** <YYYY-MM-DD>
    > ```
    > 🔴 **WHY IN THE DOC AND NOT IN A REGISTER: a register is a SECOND COPY of a fact that already lives in the doc, and two homes drift.** ⇒ **This one cannot.** **When the condition is met you archive the doc, and the condition goes with it — nothing to update separately, nothing to forget.**
    > ⭐ **AND YOU STILL GET THE REGISTER, DERIVED RATHER THAN MAINTAINED:** **`git grep -n "HELD-SESSION-DOC"` returns every held doc and its condition in one command.** *(A literal token rather than a prose phrase, deliberately — it cannot false-positive on ordinary writing, and it is exact.)*
    > 🔑 **ABSENCE OF THE BANNER MEANS RETIRABLE.** **A session doc without one is not held — it is a retirement candidate by default.** ⭐ **What licenses a default that harsh: *important information* can get trapped in session docs, instead of being properly persisted. And session-doc references are no longer repointed, so a wrong retirement costs a `git mv` and breaks nothing.** 🔴 **The two rules only work together.**
    > ### 🔴 BUT THAT DEFAULT IS SCOPED TO YOUR OWN LINEAGE. Another lineage's doc is never yours to retire.
    > *(Justin's ruling, 2026-08-22: **"if an ACP-lineage agent sees an old ACT-lineage session doc, I *don't* want him just retiring it. I want him sending a message to ACT to figure out what he needs to do with it."**)*
    > **The top-level lineages are `ACP` and `ACT` (and, at the moment — 2026-08-22 — `ACv`, but that'll be short-lived) — that is the whole list.** ⇒ **When a doc belongs to a lineage that is not yours: BANNER that it is only being held for its owner to evaluate, message that owner's inbox, and move on. Do NOT retire it, and do NOT judge its contents.**
    > 🔑 **Why the default approach is wrong across a lineage boundary, and it is not politeness: they're doing this culling process too, so unbannered work is likely simply *in-flight*.** **You cannot see another lane's live work** — its worktrees, its unspun briefs, what it is mid-way through. **An unbannered doc means "nobody on MY side is holding this," never "nobody is."**
    > ⚠️ **And the asymmetry that makes this worth a rule: retiring your own stale doc costs a `git mv`; retiring theirs can strand a lane whose owner is not in the room to object.**
    > ⚠️ **THE CONDITION MUST BE TESTABLE IN UNDER A MINUTE.** *"Still in play"* and *"might be useful"* are true of almost everything and expire silently. ⚠️ **And the tell that you are holding the wrong kind of doc: if the condition is *"once its content is rehomed,"* you have a misfiled REAL doc — move it to its department's folder instead.**
    > ⚠️ **OWNER IS A LINEAGE, NEVER AN INSTANCE** — an instance dies at the end of its session, so an instance-owned condition is orphaned the moment it is written.
    > ### ⏳ THE AGING CHECK — run it on every banner you meet
    > **If a held doc is more than a week old AND you cannot name a specific thing already on someone's list that would satisfy its condition, ask Justin whether its content should be persisted somewhere durable instead of held here.**
    > 🔑 **The test is not *"will this take a while."* It is *"is anything actually going to make this true?"*** **A condition waiting on scheduled work is fine and may wait months.** **A condition waiting on nobody is a doc being STORED, not held** — and its content belongs in a backlog, a Step or an ADR, after which the doc retires.
    - 🔴 **BEFORE YOU RETIRE A DOC, DISCHARGE WHAT IT ROUTED OUT. The banner asks whether the DOC is still needed; this asks whether its CONTENTS landed.** For every item the doc hands to someone else — an *"owed," "routed to," "still open,"* or *"deliberately not done"* section — **name where that item now lives that is NOT this doc.** A Step number, an ADR, a tracker row, a line in a durable doc. ⚠️ **"It was routed to X" is not a destination — X is a person, and people are not storage.** 🔑 **An instruction that can be answered *"yes, I swept it"* decays; one that requires NAMING A DESTINATION cannot be satisfied vacuously.**
      - ⚠️ **AND RE-CHECK THAT THE ITEM IS STILL OPEN BEFORE YOU RE-FILE IT. AN OWED ITEM'S AGE IS NOT EVIDENCE THAT IT IS STILL OPEN** — a closed lane's brief hides ALREADY-FIXED work exactly as readily as it hides untracked work, because a stale finding reads as still-open. **Re-checking one costs a `git log`.** *(2026-09-01: of four items on one closed brief's owed list, one was a real untracked defect, two were genuinely open, and one had been FIXED the day after the finding was written — and had already reached Justin, from two independent lanes, as a live problem.)*
      - 🔑 **Why this is the gap and not a nicety: a doc's OUTBOUND routing is the one thing nothing else in this checklist covers.** The bullet below asks whether anything points AT the doc; the banner asks whether the doc is still needed. **Neither asks what the doc handed to someone else.** *(A scan across sixteen working docs found NINE carrying an owed-items section.)*
    - Then scan back through `docs/sessions/` AND `docs/working/` for recent docs this session has superseded (an old handoff replaced by a newer one; a lane brief whose work is settled and absorbed). If you find candidates, **list them for Justin and get his explicit OK before archiving any to the appropriate subfolder in `docs/sessions/historical/`.** Some old docs are still in play — he wants veto power. **Never move a session or working doc silently.**
    - **Why a bare "still in play" is not enough:** *"still referenced"* and *"might be useful"* are true of almost anything and expire silently. **A held doc with no condition attached is a doc nobody will ever retire**, because the next instance inherits the caution without the reasoning and has no way to test whether it still applies. ⚠️ **That is how a working folder becomes an archive nobody dares touch.**
    - 🔑 **If the ONLY thing holding a doc alive is that something references it, that is not a reason to keep it — it is a task: MOVE THE REFERENCED MATERIAL TO A PROPER HOME.** A durable fact living in a session doc is on a timer either way.
    - ⚠️ **Only automatically retire a doc if it's 100% clear that it should be retired.** **Anything needing a judgement call is a RECOMMENDATION for Justin, not an action** — and either recommend it now, or it must be put into your handoff with its condition, where he can rule on it in one line.
11. **`LEARNINGS.md` — the MECHANICS only. The routing decision is step 5e's and is NOT repeated here.** *(Rewritten 2026-08-13. It used to read "add appropriate cross-project patterns or insights," which restated 5e's obligation at lower quality — so a reader did both, and the vaguer instruction won. **Two statements of one obligation is how a careful rule gets averaged away.** 5e decides *whether and where*; this step is *how to write it once you have decided it goes here*.)*
    - **Only what passed 5e's test arrives here** — the version another repo could act on. **If you are still holding a lane-local lesson at this step, you skipped 5e; go back.**
    - **Write it as an UN-NUMBERED APPENDAGE at the bottom of the Unpromoted section, and do NOT promote it during the lock.** You are deep in this session's context and cannot see every surface the learning should reach — that judgment belongs to `#sweep`, with fresh eyes. **Numbers are assigned at promotion, not at capture.** *(This is `LEARNINGS.md`'s own header rule; it lives there and is restated here only because this is the moment someone would violate it.)*
    - ⚠️ **`AGENT_PATTERNS.md` NO LONGER EXISTS** — collapsed into `LEARNINGS.md` on 2026-08-12 and **retired outright on 2026-08-19**. There is nothing to route to and no redirect to land on.
12. ⚫ **RETIRED — `AGENT_PATTERNS.md` was COLLAPSED into `LEARNINGS.md` on 2026-08-12, and the file itself was RETIRED on 2026-08-19** (both Justin's rulings; the collapsed entries live in `LEARNINGS.md`'s Unpromoted section under *"Absorbed from `AGENT_PATTERNS.md`"*, and the retired file is at `docs/historical/AGENT_PATTERNS.md`). **Agent-building learnings now go to `LEARNINGS.md` — i.e. step 11 above, which is the whole of it.** ⚠️ **The step NUMBER is kept rather than deleted, so references to steps 13–19 do not silently shift.**
13. **Linear** — Update the status of any of your tickets that need it. If this session produced work that doesn't belong in a build, project, or session doc, create a ticket per `evryn-team-workspace/shared/protocols/linear-protocol.md`. If you changed something in someone else's domain, send them a ticket so they know.
14. **Bitwarden reminder** — If `.env` was modified, remind Justin: "Hey, we updated .env — remember to re-upload to Bitwarden." (Files in `.gitignore` exist only on the local machine — git won't save them. Most credentials can be regenerated from service dashboards, but it's time-consuming. Prevention beats cure.)
15. **Mailbox check** — Peek at `dc-to-ac.md` and `dc-architecture-notes-for-ac.md` in any repo you touched this session. If there's content you haven't absorbed, absorb it now.
16. **Operator guide** — If anything built or changed this session affects how Justin operates Evryn, update the relevant repo's `docs/operator-guide.md`. DC flags operator-relevant changes in dc-to-ac.md; AC updates the guide.
17. **Database — backups + schema-reference.** Pro takes daily auto-backups (primary). For the archival layer: if the newest `pg_dump` in `evryn-backend/backups/` is more than a week old, take a fresh one — method in `backups/README.md`. **And if a schema migration ran this session** (added / renamed / dropped a table or column, new RPC / trigger / RLS), **re-pull `evryn-backend/docs/schema-reference.md` from Supabase** — it's a generated snapshot, not authored prose, so it drifts silently precisely because nobody owns re-pulling it. (A new `public` table also needs `GRANT … TO service_role` + `ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` — see the routing protocol, change-type 2.)
18. **Auto-memory hygiene** — Check `.claude/projects/*/memory/MEMORY.md`. AC does not use auto-memory (see CLAUDE.md Auto-Memory Hygiene). If anything landed there accidentally, promote it to persistent docs or clear it. The file should contain only the "DO NOT WRITE HERE" notice.
19. **Settings.local.json cleanup** — Check for `.claude/settings.local.json` in the current repo. This file silently accumulates one-off command approvals at runtime. Delete it if it exists — permissions belong in `.claude/settings.json` (in git), not in local overrides. If it contains secrets (API keys, UUIDs that were auto-saved), flag to Justin before deleting.

    **Worktree hygiene.** For each repo you (or the agents you drove) touched, run `git -C <repo> worktree list`. **Reap stale worktrees** — any whose branch is fully merged into the default branch and whose tree is clean: `git worktree remove <path>` + `git branch -d <branch>` (the lowercase `-d` self-guards, refusing an unmerged branch — if it refuses, the branch has unmerged work; stop and surface it). Leave only the canonical tree + any standing per-agent worktree. The *per-loop* reap (remove right after a merge) lives in `_evryn-meta/CLAUDE.md` (Worktree & Branch Discipline); this #lock step is the periodic safety-net for leftovers that slipped through.
20. **Fragment sweep — a *careful, thorough* pass, not a "quick" one.** The temptation at the end of a long session is to skim this as a formality — **resist that.** The category-based steps above catch what you *remember* happened; this pass exists to catch what you *forgot you forgot*, and you only catch that by actually re-reading the whole conversation, beat by beat, with attention. A rushed fragment sweep is the same as no fragment sweep — the fragments it's meant to catch are exactly the ones a skim misses. **Budget real time for it.** Scroll back through the full conversation and look for: intentions that got derailed, decisions that only live in chat, action items acknowledged but never recorded, things Justin asked for that got handled conversationally but never persisted. Resolve or route anything you find.
21. ➡️ **MOVED TO `docs/protocols/packout-protocol.md` — SUBAGENT CLOSE-OUT.** *(2026-09-02, Justin's direction.)*

    🔑 **Why it moved: its own first clause always scoped it to *"if you are an orchestrator `#lock`ing before your own re-spin"* — which is a PACKOUT, not a lock.** **Most locks are mid-session or end-of-night with no re-spin following, and this step is long and heavy**, so every one of those was paying for a gate that did not apply to it. ⚠️ **An expensive checkpoint is one that quietly stops getting run** — that is the whole reason `#packout` exists as a separate command.

    ⚠️ **If you ARE packing out, this is still a HARD GATE and nothing about it softened.** **Subagent resume is session-bound: every agent you spawned becomes permanently unreachable the moment your session ends, and a returned report is not persistence.**

    📌 **The step NUMBER is kept rather than deleted, so references to step 22 and 23 do not silently shift** — same convention as step 12 above.

22. **Pause for Justin — hard stop. Do not commit yet.** Wait for Justin's clear and present explicit command to "push" or "commit" before this specific commit or push.

    **The test:** *"Did Justin's **most recent message** contain a specific **command** to commit or push?"* If no, summarize what's ready and pause. Workflow instructions ("ping me when you're done," "do the lock," "finish this up," "handle it") describe the work, not the commits — they do not authorize commits. Each commit needs its own affirmative opt-in in the immediately preceding turn; prior authorizations do not stack.

    Failure to do this has been shown in the past to **break** important things.
23. **Commit and push** — Get everything to remote immediately.
